newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-RAVANELLI SEARCHING FOR A PLACE IN HISTORY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-RAVANELLI SEARCHING FOR A PLACE IN HISTORY.

text.p: Nothing illustrates the complete transformation of Middlesbrough from perennial also-rans to possible trophy-hunters than the audacious signing of Italian international striker Fabrizio Ravanelli in the summer.

His move from European champions Juventus to an unglamorous 121-year-old club in the north-east of England which has never won anything, made headlines worldwide and put Middlesbrough's name up there with the likes of Manchester United, Liverpool and Newcastle United as one of the main contenders in English soccer.

It was greeted with far more astonishment than the much-heralded arrival of Brazilian "wonderkid" Juninho a year ago, and with far more excitement than the opening of Middlesbrough's new Riverside Stadium, the most tangible image of the club's change in status.

But Ravanelli's move was something else. Suddenly hundreds of men around the tough, gritty industrial city where local unemployment far exceeds the national average, began sporting dyed grey haircuts styled just like the man nicknamed "The White Feather" -- not to mention walking around in Italian-style suits.
The Italian flag began flying out of a lot more windows than just pizza parlours and the entire city was given a boost.

But what made him come? Why would a player of Ravanelli's class, experience and stature, at the peak of his career after scoring for Juventus in the European Cup final in May, become the subject of one of the most surreal transfers ever?
"I could have gone to Liverpool, Manchester United or Rangers but it was more of a challenge to win something here -- and to play for Bryan Robson," the 27-year-old striker said.

"I know Middlesbrough have never won anything but Mr Robson told me about the fans, about how enthusiastic and passionate they are and how desperate they are for success. I was also impressed by Robson. I remember him as a great player and it was a great honour for me to be wanted by him and to play for him."

Ravanelli could hardly have made a better start to his new career, hitting a debut hat-trick in a 3-3 draw against Liverpool and then keeping up his strike rate so that he now has 13 goals in all competitions and heads the scoring tables.

"The pace here is very fast, that is the main difference from Italy, and although the play may not be as technical as say in Italy, or Brazil, it does not matter. A lot of the technique is performed at very high speed which makes the game in England very exciting," he added.

Ravanelli scored 41 goals in 111 games for Juventus and admits he was surprised when they let him leave. He thought coach Marcello Lippi was going to make him captain after Gianluca Vialli left for Chelsea but when he realised that Juve were prepared to do a deal, he was determined to go as soon as possible.
Robson said that he used the example of Parma to sell Middlesbrough to Ravanelli.

"When I first talked to him I mentioned Parma and the way they had come into Serie A from Serie B at the turn of the decade and gone on to win European and domestic trophies every year since promotion.
"I told him that 'Boro had never won a major trophy and that he could go into the history books. I think that appealed to him."
Ravanelli is earning a reported 24,000 pounds ($39,080) a week at Middlesbrough, which is far more than many people in the city earn in a year.

But if he carries on scoring at the rate he has started at, and if he were to score the winner in Sunday's derby against Newcastle United at St James' Park, there would not be many Middlesbrough fans begrudging him a penny of that money.

Ravanelli will be one of a number of high profile imports playing on Sunday. Newcastle have the Colombian Faustino Asprilla, the Frenchman David Ginola, Belgian Phillipe Albert and Czech keeper Pavel Srnicek in their line-up, while Middlesbrough have Juninho and Emerson from Brazil as well as Ravanelli, whose mere presence seems to raise any game he is in to a higher plane.
While Middlesbrough are paying him a king's ransom, he knows he is under pressure to perform and seems to have heard a calling that some of the other foreign players have not had.
In many ways everything is in place for Middlesbrough to end more than a century without success with a trophy.
They have the stadium, the manager, they have Juninho and Emerson from Brazil and now they have the White Feather.
The fans don't want any more excuses. They want results, they want trophies and they want goals. And if anyone can deliver them, Ravanelli can.
